speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Over the past 10 years, we have seen improvements in lighting technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) have become more prevalent on the commercial market and have transformed the market for lighting.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The lifespan of an LED is longer than that of a traditional incandescent light bulb.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: LEDs give out less heat, important in a tropical country like Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: LEDs, generally, are more energy-efficient than other types of light bulbs or even fluorescent lamps, and their energy efficiency is getting better year-by-year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They are an example of how science and technology are improving people's lives − new solutions to old problems.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, there are many different types of LED lights, each with slightly different shades of colour, even different shades of white.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: To describe the shades of white, the experts use the phrase "colour temperature".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is not the temperature of the light bulb, but if I may use the language of scientists, it is the temperature of an ideal black-body radiator giving out light of comparable colour to the light source.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You might call it the colour of "red-hot", "yellow-hot" or "white-hot", even if the LED light itself does not give out much heat.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we have some LEDs which give out a yellowish, warmer, more natural-looking white, or colour temperature of around 3,000 Kelvin.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some have a harsher white colour, with a little bit of blue light as well, or a colour temperature closer to 4,500 Kelvin or more.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Over the years, it has become easier for us to light up the night, but this has also brought to light new challenges as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, Mr Deputy Speaker, exposure to light has been reported to suppress the production of melatonin.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Melatonin is a hormone produced by the body that influences the body's own biological rhythms, what we call the circadian rhythms that tell our bodies when we feel sleepy and when we feel awake.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: While any kind of visible light can suppress the production of melatonin, we know from research at Harvard University that blue light, in particular, has a stronger effect than other kinds of light.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, blue light suppresses the production of melatonin for about twice as long as green light of comparable brightness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It shifts the circadian rhythm − the sleeping, waking rhythm − by three hours instead of just one-and-a-half hours.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some researchers have even raised concerns about whether shifting this circadian rhythm can affect eating habits and, in turn, the risk of obesity and diabetes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The research is ongoing but questions like these are being talked about.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also know that modern fluorescent lights and LEDs produce more blue light than traditional light bulbs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we look at the US and Europe, increasingly, there are policy suggestions proposing that the colour of light is important, especially at night.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Public Health recommends that LED lamps should have less blue light component.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The American Medical Association has also called for a reduction in the amount of blue light component in LED lights.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Harvard Medical School, in their Harvard Health Letter, has pointed out that having too much blue light at night may not be optimal for health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am grateful to experts, such as Prof Michael Chee from the Duke-NUS Medical School, for highlighting some of these pointers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even in the commercial sector, even among the companies that build your portable devices, such as the Apple iPhone, has a "night mode", where the colour of the display shifts to a more yellow shade of white, with less blue light emitted.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is because in our built-up housing estates, the colour of night is shaded by what kind of lighting we choose.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Corridor light in our housing estates and in our void decks can shine into living rooms and bedrooms.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, it is also important that our housing estates are energy efficient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And our housing estates must also, at the same time, be brightly lit enough so that all residents, especially our vulnerable and elderly, are able to move about safely at night.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Currently, both the pure white light and warmer yellow-white light LEDs would satisfy this IEC criteria.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, at the same time, given the discussions going on in the US and Europe, it is quite possible that the consensus may be shifting in favour of warm yellow-white LED lights, lights which are less pure white but have a warmer yellow-white colour.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What kind of power output is needed for a pure white LED to look as bright as a warm yellow LED, how to calibrate this, how to have these standards?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And once these standards have been studied by HDB, they could be shared with other agencies as well as the private sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I wonder if HDB's Building and Research Institute could help look into this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should also encourage the Land Transport Authority (LTA) to think about having less blue light when illuminating our roads at night.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is important that road users can see one another, can see pedestrians, and can stay out of danger.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But within these limitations, we should look at how to reduce the amount of blue light given out by LED lights.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And Deputy Speaker, all these could be part of a shared design language that shapes the aesthetics of our housing estates and our shared spaces throughout our little red dot.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, as a little red dot on the Equator, we have 12 hours of daylight each day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The rest is night; one half of our existence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it matters how we light the night.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: May we always choose well and always seek the right kind of illumination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Deputy Speaker, I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng that night lighting has an impact on the everyday lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our lighting must, first, be functional, for drivers on our expressways to passers-by along our HDB estate corridors, night lighting must be calibrated to suit their different needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It should positively shape how we perceive and interact with our estates and public spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is important, given how pervasive night lighting is in a dense built-up city like Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To achieve this, one of the specifications we take into account is the light colour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And those of you who have bought fluorescent or LED lights will know that they generally come in three colours, as Dr Tan had described − warm white, pure white and cool white.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Warm white has the least amount of blue light, giving it a yellow hue and a colour temperature of about 3,000 Kelvin; pure white has a more balanced mix of blue light, giving it a natural daylight feel and a colour temperature of around 4,000 Kelvin; while cool white has the highest amount of blue light, resulting in a harsh white colour and a colour temperature of around 6,000 Kelvin.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Light colour is important for both functionality and aesthetics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For our street lighting, LTA is moving towards pure white because it offers drivers a high colour contrast, allowing them to see better at night.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In our new HDB developments, light fittings at common areas, such as corridors, also use pure white, but for a different reason.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The previous feedback garnered from residents indicated that warm white was too dim for HDB estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Light colour can affect safety, too, as Dr Tan rightly pointed out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I have explained how LTA uses light colour to improve road safety at night, for drivers and pedestrians.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Dr Tan has cited several reports which advise minimising the amount of blue light for health reasons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Based on these reports, he has suggested we use warm white in our HDB common areas and LTA street lighting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, they state that long-term or high intensity exposure to blue light can damage the retina of the human eye.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, they highlight that exposure to any light at night, especially blue light, can affect our sleep cycles by suppressing the production of a hormone called melatonin and affect our circadian rhythm or body clock.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This has been linked to impaired daytime functioning and obesity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, the first point about potential damage to the retina of the human eye is not a significant concern in Singapore, given our regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Lighting in our HDB common areas and LTA street lighting follow the globally-recognised IEC standards, which Dr Tan had articulated earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These spell out technical and safety requirements for lighting, including the safety limits for exposure to white light.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Indeed, the same report by the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health states that "commercial LED lamps represent no health risk when used correctly, in terms of the risk to human retina.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: On the second point on the impact of blue light on melatonin and our sleep cycles, as Dr Tan pointed out, there is no medical consensus on the issue as yet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The reports do not rule out the use of pure white lighting in street lighting or in public spaces like HDB common areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And the specific implications of the reports' findings on our HDB common areas and LTA street lighting are as yet unclear.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, the Harvard Medical School's Harvard Health Letter is based on studies which exposed people to blue light for six-and-a-half hours or longer, while the exposure of most Singaporeans to HDB corridors and street lighting by LTA is much shorter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Apart from changing the colour of all our lighting, there may be other ways to address this issue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Indeed, one of the possible solutions mentioned by the American Medical Association is dimming LED lighting during off-peak periods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have, in fact, already installed LED lighting with motion sensors along staircases for all Build-To-Order (BTO) projects launched since 2014, and we are testing out sensor-controlled smart lighting in the common areas of Punggol Northshore estate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Not only will this make our HDB estates more energy-efficient, but it would also minimise ambient blue-light at night.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ultimately, we must ensure that our lighting remains functional, aesthetically pleasing and safe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The light colours of HDB common areas and LTA streetlamps are carefully selected to meet the functional, safety and aesthetic needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We should only decide how best to enhance our lighting after further study on the appropriate length and intensity of blue-light exposure at night has been done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This, notwithstanding, I agree with Dr Tan that it is not too early for us to be thinking about the long-term implications of these reports on the health and safety of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will, therefore, continue to keep a close watch on the evolving research in this area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This will allow us to better decide on the appropriate light colours in different settings − be it for functional or aesthetic reasons.
